title: One word, one sentence: subject prefixes and the -na- slot
goal: Build Swahili verbs the way you couple train cars — subject, tense, root — and tell what you are doing today.
bekal: the six subject prefixes: *ni-, u-, a-, tu-, m-, wa-*
the *-na-* slot for "is doing" and for daily habits
dropping *ku-* from the dictionary form — and the six verbs that keep it

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Chuoni
dialogs.intro: Midday on the campus lawn. Juma, a young man Budi's age, sits next to him under the mango tree.

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.text: Habari za mchana! Unafanya nini hapa?
lines.id: Good afternoon! What are you doing here?
lines.literal: news of afternoon! you-are-doing what here?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'm learning Swahili. I study every day.

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.id: Very good! Where do you study?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ninajifunza hapa chuoni. Mwalimu wangu anafundisha vizuri.
lines.id: I study here at the college. My teacher teaches well.
lines.literal: I-am-teaching-myself here at-college. teacher of-me he-is-teaching well.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I understand a little. I speak very slowly.

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.text: Hakuna shida. Sisi tunaongea polepole pia.
lines.id: No problem. We speak slowly too.
lines.literal: there-is-not problem. we we-are-chatting slowly also.

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.id: I work at a hotel. I cook food.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Aa, wewe ni mpishi! Unapika nini leo?
lines.id: Oh, you're a cook! What are you cooking today?
lines.literal: ah, you are cook! you-are-cooking what today?

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.text: Ninapika samaki na wali. Wageni wanakula saa tatu.
lines.id: I'm cooking fish and rice. The guests eat at nine.
lines.literal: I-am-cooking fish and rice. guests they-are-eating hour three.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'm coming this evening. I love fish!

notes: **Ninasoma can mean "I am reading" and "I read (as a habit)".** The *-na-* slot covers two meanings that English splits apart. Context chooses, and misunderstandings almost never happen: *ninasoma sasa* (right now) versus *ninasoma kila siku* (habit).

**Kusoma means both to read and to study.** *Ninasoma kitabu* = I'm reading a book; *Ninasoma chuoni* = I study at college. For a firmer "learn" there is *kujifunza*, literally "to teach oneself" — that infix *-ji-* means "self".

**Vizuri means "well", not "good".** The *vi-* before an adjective turns it into an adverb: *nzuri* (good) → *vizuri* (well), *baya* (bad) → *vibaya* (badly). *Anafundisha vizuri* = he/she teaches well.

**Hotelini, chuoni, nyumbani — the ending -ni means "in/at".** Attach it to any place noun: *hoteli* → *hotelini* (at the hotel), *chuo* → *chuoni* (at college), *soko* → *sokoni* (at the market). This ending is taken apart fully in unit 8; for now just use these as whole words.

**Hakuna shida = "there is no problem".** This phrase, together with its cousin *hakuna matata*, is the most famous Swahili phrase in the world — and it really is used every day. *Hakuna* means "there is not", and you'll build it yourself in unit 8.

grammars.title: The verb train: subject + tense + root
body: Swahili verbs don't conjugate — they are **assembled**. Three cars, always in the same order, with no spaces between them:
**subject prefix + tense slot + root**. *Ni* + *na* + *soma* = *ninasoma*. Change the front car, the subject changes. Change the middle car, the tense changes. The root is never touched.
after: The pronoun (*mimi*, *wewe*, …) is almost always **dropped**, because the prefix already carries the subject. *Ninasoma* already means "I read". The pronoun is used when you want to stress or contrast: *Mimi ninasoma, wewe unalala* — "I'm studying, you're sleeping".
Watch the stress: it's always on the second-to-last syllable, so it **shifts by itself** as the word grows. *SO-ma* → *ni-na-SO-ma* → *ni-na-ku-SO-ma*. Nothing to memorize.

The third-person prefix *a-* merges with the next vowel: *a- + -elewa* becomes **anaelewa** (not *aelewa*), and the *m-* prefix for "you (pl.)" stands alone as a syllable: *mnasoma* is pronounced m-na-SO-ma.

grammars.title: The ku- that drops off — and the six verbs that keep it
body: The dictionary form of every verb starts with **ku-**, which means "to…": *kusoma* (to read), *kupika* (to cook). As soon as a subject prefix is attached, that *ku-* is **dropped**.
after: The reason is purely sound: the root is too short to stand alone. *Ni-na-la* is awkward to say and the stress lands nowhere, so *ku-* stays as a prop. One-syllable verbs can be counted on your fingers — the six in this table plus *kufa* (to die) — and they are all words you'll use every day, so they will stick by themselves.
*Kwenda* has one concession: the form *ninaenda* is also correct and is in fact heard more often in everyday speech. Both are fine.
⚠️ Don't confuse this prop *ku-* with the *ku-* that means "you" as an object (*ninakupenda* = I love you). The second one sits in a different slot and is taken apart in unit 15.

blocks.text: Almost all end in **-a**, and that is no accident: native Swahili verbs always end in *-a*. Those ending in *-i*, *-e* or *-u* — *kufikiri* (to think), *kusamehe* (to forgive), *kujibu* (to answer) — are almost always loans from Arabic, and the difference only shows up when the sentence is negated in unit 4.

sections.title: Sasa, leo, kila siku — when and how often

blocks.text: All of them stand **after the verb**, never in front of it: *Ninasoma kila siku*, *Anapika haraka*, *Tunacheza pamoja*. That is the usual position in English too.

*Polepole* is the favorite word of East Africa, and it means more than "slowly". It is an attitude to life: *Pole pole ndio mwendo* — "slowly, slowly is the way to walk". If someone says it to you when you're in a rush, it isn't a rebuke, it's an invitation to breathe.
